New York Transfer Tax: State, NYC and Local Rates, and Who Pays

Cash Home Buyers in New York
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New York Transfer Tax sale
  • Turn the New York Transfer Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a New York House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

New York charges a state real estate transfer tax of $2 for each $500 of consideration, and the seller pays it. Some places add their own taxes. This guide lists only what we confirmed on official pages.

What the official sources say

  • NY state real estate transfer tax: $2 for each $500 or fractional part of consideration on each conveyance of real property when consideration exceeds $500 (i.e., $2 per $500 = 0.4%). For 1-3 family houses and individual residential condo units, and conveyances under $500,000, consideration excludes the value of any lien/encumbrance remaining at conveyance. (NY Tax Law §1402(a); source)
  • Additional $1.25 per $500 of consideration applies to conveyances within a city of 1,000,000+ population when residential consideration is $3,000,000 or more (or $2,000,000+ for other property). 'Residential real property' includes a 1-3 family house, an individual condo unit, or a cooperative apartment unit. (NY Tax Law §1402(a)(2); source)
  • Additional ('mansion') tax: 1% of consideration on conveyance of residential real property (1-3 family house, individual condo unit, co-op unit) when consideration for the entire conveyance is $1,000,000 or more. Paid by the grantee; if grantee fails to pay or is exempt, the grantor has the duty to pay and liability is joint and several. (NY Tax Law §1402-a(a)-(b); source)
  • NYS Tax Dept: base transfer tax $2 per $500 of consideration (consideration > $500); additional 'mansion' tax 1% for residences at $1M+. For NYC conveyances from July 1, 2019: extra $1.25 per $500 for residential >= $3M (or other property >= $2M), plus a supplemental tax on residential >= $2M at incremental rates between 0.25% and 2.9% (rates in Form TP-584-NYC-I). (NYS DTF 'Real estate transfer tax' page (reviewed June 1, 2026); source)
  • Who pays: base tax and additional base tax are paid by the grantor (seller) (buyer pays if seller doesn't or is exempt); mansion tax and NYC supplemental tax are paid by the buyer (seller pays if buyer fails/is exempt, joint and several). (NYS DTF 'Real estate transfer tax' - Who pays the tax; source)
  • Filing: outside NYC, file Form TP-584 with the county clerk where the property is located; form and tax due no later than the 15th day after delivery of the deed. NYC conveyances use Form TP-584-NYC. If deed is not recorded, file with the Tax Department directly by the 15th day. (NYS DTF 'Real estate transfer tax' - File and pay tax; source)
  • Nontaxable conveyances include: conveyances without consideration/bona fide gifts, to secure a debt, tax-sale conveyances, partition deeds, Bankruptcy Act conveyances, mere change of identity with no change in beneficial ownership. 'Conveyance' includes mortgage foreclosure and transfer in lieu of foreclosure but excludes conveyance pursuant to devise, bequest or inheritance. (NYS DTF 'Real estate transfer tax' - Exemptions and Definitions; source)
  • LLC rule: when an LLC is seller or buyer of a building with up to four dwelling units, TP-584 cannot be accepted without documentation identifying names and addresses of all members, managers and authorized persons (down to natural persons). (NYS DTF 'Real estate transfer tax' - Conveyances to or from an LLC; source)
  • NYC RPTT (city tax, Admin Code Title 11 Ch. 21; enabling Tax Law 1201(b)): residential 1-3 family house/condo/co-op: 1% if value $500,000 or less, 1.425% if more than $500,000; all other transfers: 1.425% if $500,000 or less, 2.625% if more. Applies when sale/transfer is more than $25,000. Return and payment due within 30 days after transfer; filed through ACRIS (NYC-RPT). Executor's deed per will terms is exempt but reportable; executor deed in connection with a sale is taxable. (NYC Dept of Finance, Real Property Transfer Tax (RPTT) page; source)
  • Mount Vernon: state enabling statute authorizes the city to impose a deed transfer tax at a rate not to exceed 1.5% of consideration, may allow lien deductions and an exemption up to $100,000; payment/return may be required as a condition precedent to recording. Actual adopted local rate/exemption not confirmed. (NY Tax Law §1205(b) (rev. 2025-12-12); source)
  • Peekskill: state enabling statute authorizes the city to impose a deed transfer tax at a rate not to exceed 1% of consideration, with optional lien deductions and exemption up to $100,000; contracts before Sept 1, 2007 not covered. Actual adopted local rate not confirmed. (NY Tax Law §1206(b); source)

Get My Cash Offer →

Filing and recording

  • Form TP-584 (Combined Real Estate Transfer Tax Return, Credit Line Mortgage Certificate, and Certification of Exemption from Payment of Estimated Personal Income Tax) is filed with the county clerk for property outside NYC (TP-584-NYC inside NYC) by the 15th day after delivery of the deed. (NYS DTF real estate transfer tax page; source)
  • Form RP-5217 (Real Property Transfer Report) filing fee is generally $125 for residential (1-3 family, rural residence, residential condo) and farm properties and $250 for all other properties; collected by the county clerk. (NYS DTF 'Filing Fees for Form RP-5217' (updated May 18, 2023); source)

What we could not confirm

  • The actual local transfer tax rates in Mount Vernon and Peekskill. State law only sets the maximum.

New York transfer tax FAQ

Who pays the New York transfer tax?

The seller pays the base state tax. The buyer pays the mansion tax and the NYC supplemental tax, as described on the Department of Taxation and Finance page.

How do I file the transfer tax return?

Outside New York City, file Form TP-584 with the county clerk where the property sits. It is due no later than the 15th day after the deed is delivered.

Is an inherited house taxed on transfer?

State law excludes conveyances by devise, bequest or inheritance. NYC treats an executor deed given in connection with a sale as taxable.

How much is the New York transfer tax when you sell a house?

The state charges $2 for every $500 of consideration, or fractional part of $500, on a conveyance of real property worth more than $500. That works out to 0.4% of the price, and the seller pays it unless the contract says otherwise.

The rate comes from Tax Law section 1402. To see how the "fractional part" language plays out, take a $400,000 house: that is 800 blocks of $500, so the tax is $1,600. A $400,100 price adds one more block and the tax becomes $1,602. Sellers of one- to three-family houses and individual condominium units, and anyone selling for under $500,000, subtract the value of any lien that stays on the property after the sale, so a loan the buyer assumes does not raise the taxable amount.

What extra transfer taxes apply to expensive homes?

Two add-ons exist. The "mansion tax" is 1% of the sale price on a residence where consideration is $1 million or more, and in New York City a further state charge applies to the top of the market.

  • Mansion tax: 1% on a one-, two- or three-family house, condominium unit or co-op unit selling for $1,000,000 or more. The buyer pays it.
  • City additional base tax: $1.25 per $500 within New York City when residential consideration is $3 million or more, or $2 million or more for other property. The seller pays it.
  • City supplemental tax: an incremental rate between 0.25% and 2.9% on residential sales of $2 million or more in the city, published in the instructions to Form TP-584-NYC. The buyer pays it.

These city charges apply to conveyances from July 1, 2019 forward, other than deals made under a binding written contract signed on or before April 1, 2019, according to the Tax Department.

Who pays the transfer tax, the seller or the buyer?

The seller pays the base tax, and the buyer pays the mansion tax and the city supplemental tax. The Tax Department adds that each side picks up the other's share if the responsible party does not pay or is exempt.

Who owes each state-level transfer tax, from the NYS Department of Taxation and Finance (page reviewed June 1, 2026)
TaxRatePaid by
Base tax$2 per $500 of considerationSeller (grantor)
Additional base tax, NYC only$1.25 per $500 at the $3 million or $2 million thresholdsSeller
Mansion tax1% at $1 million or more, residentialBuyer (grantee)
Supplemental tax, NYC only0.25% to 2.9% at $2 million or more, residentialBuyer

A buyer can agree in the contract to pay the base tax, but the state says it cannot be passed to the buyer in any other way. Where the buyer covers a residential base tax by contract, that payment is left out when computing the taxable amount. If one side steps in for the other, the tax becomes a joint and several liability, though the buyer who paid the seller's share has a claim against the seller for recovery.

How and when is the transfer tax filed and paid?

Outside New York City you file Form TP-584 with the county clerk where the property is located, with the tax, no later than the 15th day after the deed is delivered.

If the deed will not be recorded, the form and payment go straight to the Tax Department by the same 15th-day deadline. Conveyances inside New York City use Form TP-584-NYC. Nonresident sellers must also work out the gain on the sale and pay any estimated personal income tax due, unless they qualify for one of the exemptions printed on Schedule D of the form.

Read the instructions on the form itself and confirm the current address for mailed filings, since the Tax Department directs filers to the address on the form.

Is there a transfer tax in New York City?

Yes. New York City adds its own Real Property Transfer Tax on sales, grants, assignments and surrenders of real property, and on transfers of at least 50% of an entity that owns or leases property. The city's Department of Finance says it is usually paid as part of closing costs.

City returns are built online through ACRIS, the Automated City Register Information System. Both grantor and grantee must sign the return, and a party who does not sign may owe non-filer penalties. A late return adds 5% of the tax for each month, up to 25%, and late payment adds 0.5% per month, up to 25%, with a combined cap of 5% in any one month. The Department of Finance allows written extension requests of up to 30 days, received before the due date.

For the city rates themselves, use the Department of Finance page linked in the sources, since the rate schedule changes with the type of property and the price.

Do any local governments outside New York City add a transfer tax?

Some do. One documented example is the Town of Southampton on Long Island, where the Peconic Bay Region Community Preservation Fund tax is a 2.5% transfer tax that includes a 0.5% Peconic Bay Community Housing Fund component, according to the town's own FAQ.

Southampton exempts the first $100,000 of a vacant, unimproved residential parcel and the first $400,000 of an improved residential parcel where consideration is $2,000,000 or less, and there is a first-time home buyer exemption. The title closer generally collects the tax at closing and files it with the deed at the Suffolk County Clerk's Office. If you sell in a town on the east end of Long Island, ask your closing attorney whether the town you are in has the same fund and which exemptions apply to you. Anywhere else in the state, ask your town or village clerk whether a local transfer tax exists.

Which transfers are not taxed?

The Tax Department lists many conveyances that carry no transfer tax, and several matter to families selling inherited or distressed homes.

  • Gifts and other conveyances without consideration that are not part of a sale.
  • Conveyances that secure a debt, and conveyances given in connection with a tax sale.
  • Deeds of partition and conveyances under the federal Bankruptcy Act.
  • A mere change of identity or form of ownership with no change in who benefits.

A transfer by devise, bequest or inheritance is not a taxable conveyance, but the definition does include mortgage foreclosure and a transfer in lieu of foreclosure. Governmental bodies including New York State, the United States and the United Nations are exempt, though a buyer from them owes the tax.

What if an LLC is buying or selling the house?

The county clerk cannot accept Form TP-584 for a building of up to four dwelling units when an LLC is the seller or buyer unless the filing includes documentation of every member, manager and other authorized person. If a member is itself an entity, the names go down the ownership chain until real people are reached.

Investors who buy houses through LLCs should expect this paperwork at every closing. New York City has a similar rule for city returns, requiring an enhanced member list on Form NYC-RPT for deed transfers of one- to four-family buildings.

More questions about New York Transfer Tax

Does the seller pay the New York transfer tax?

Yes, the seller pays the base tax of $2 per $500 of consideration. The buyer pays the mansion tax and the city supplemental tax, and a buyer can agree by contract to cover the base tax.

What is the transfer tax on a $500,000 house in New York?

It is $2,000. A $500,000 price is 1,000 blocks of $500 at $2 each. A sale at or over $1 million also triggers the 1% mansion tax, which the buyer pays.

Where do I file Form TP-584?

File it with the county clerk where the property sits, together with the tax, no later than the 15th day after the deed is delivered. If the deed will not be recorded, send it to the Tax Department by that date.

Do I owe transfer tax on a house I inherited?

No tax applies to the transfer of the house to you by devise, bequest or inheritance, because those are not conveyances under the state definition. When you later sell it, the sale is a conveyance and the base tax applies as usual.

Is a foreclosure a taxable transfer?

The state's definition of conveyance includes mortgage foreclosure and a transfer in lieu of foreclosure. Conveyances given in connection with a tax sale are listed among the nontaxable ones.

The New York mansion tax is 1 percent of the price on residential sales of $1,000,000 or more, and the buyer pays it.

What the official sources say

  • Additional $1.25 per $500 of consideration applies to conveyances within a city of 1,000,000+ population when residential consideration is $3,000,000 or more (or $2,000,000+ for other property). 'Residential real property' includes a 1-3 family house, an individual condo unit, or a cooperative apartment unit. (NY Tax Law §1402(a)(2); source)

  • NYS Tax Dept: base transfer tax $2 per $500 of consideration (consideration > $500); additional 'mansion' tax 1% for residences at $1M+. For NYC conveyances from July 1, 2019: extra $1.25 per $500 for residential >= $3M (or other property >= $2M), plus a supplemental tax on residential >= $2M at incremental rates between 0.25% and 2.9% (rates in Form TP-584-NYC-I). (NYS DTF 'Real estate transfer tax' - Who pays the tax; source)

Applies when sale/transfer is more than $25,000. Return and payment due within 30 days after transfer; filed through ACRIS (NYC-RPT). Actual adopted local rate not confirmed. (NY Tax Law §1206(b); source)

New York mansion tax FAQ

Who pays the mansion tax?

The buyer pays it. If the buyer fails to pay or is exempt, the seller can become liable, according to the Department of Taxation and Finance.

What price triggers the mansion tax?

One percent applies when the consideration for the whole conveyance of residential property is $1,000,000 or more.

What is the New York mansion tax?

The mansion tax is a 1 percent charge on the sale of a New York residence when the consideration for the whole conveyance reaches $1 million. It sits on top of the regular state transfer tax and is written into Tax Law section 1402-a.

The 1 percent applies to the consideration, or the part of it that belongs to the residential property. Once a sale crosses the line, the tax is computed on the full residential amount, not only on the dollars above $1 million. A $1,200,000 three-family house, for example, produces $12,000 of mansion tax, which is the figure the state's own FAQ publication uses for that case.

For a seller in New York, the practical point is that the tax is normally the buyer's bill, yet the seller can end up answerable for it. That makes it worth understanding before a contract is signed on any home priced near seven figures.

Who pays the mansion tax when a house sells?

The buyer pays the mansion tax. Section 1402-a(b) puts the duty on the grantee, and the Department of Taxation and Finance repeats that on its real estate transfer tax page.

If the buyer fails to pay, or is exempt, the duty shifts to the seller. In that case the liability is joint and several, meaning the state may collect the whole amount from either party.

The other taxes in a New York sale follow a different split, as the table shows.

Who pays each New York transfer tax (source: NYS Department of Taxation and Finance, real estate transfer tax page)
TaxRate or triggerPaid by
Base transfer tax$2 per $500 of considerationSeller
Mansion tax1% when residential consideration is $1 million or moreBuyer
Additional base tax (New York City only)$1.25 per $500 on residential sales of $3 million or more, or other property at $2 million or moreSeller
Supplemental tax (New York City only)0.25% to 2.9% on residential sales of $2 million or moreBuyer

Which properties count as residential?

Residential real property is any premises that is or may be used in whole or in part as a personal residence. The statute names three kinds in particular:

  • a one, two or three-family house;
  • an individual condominium unit;
  • a cooperative apartment unit.

The state's Publication 577 adds detail that surprises owners. A seasonal cottage that sits empty or is rented for part of the year is still residential. So is a house the seller never lived in, as long as it is or may be rented to others as a home.

The same publication draws a line at building size. A structure with a store on the ground floor and three apartments above has four units, so it is not a three-family house. A ten-apartment building does not qualify even if the seller lived in one apartment.

How does the $1 million threshold get measured?

The threshold is measured against everything the buyer pays or owes for the property, not only the cash that changes hands. Consideration includes the price, the cancellation of any debt, and the amount of any mortgage or lien, whether the buyer assumes it or takes the property subject to it.

Several rules in Publication 577 decide close cases:

  • No lien deduction. The base transfer tax lets a seller of a one to three-family house subtract a continuing lien, but the mansion tax does not. A condo that sells for $1 million with a $400,000 mortgage assumed is taxed on the full $1 million for mansion tax purposes, while the seller's base tax is figured on $600,000.
  • Seller costs the buyer absorbs count as price. In the publication's example, a $975,000 sale becomes $1,033,500 once the buyer agrees to cover a $58,500 brokerage obligation, and $10,335 of mansion tax follows.
  • Related sellers are added together. Two co-owners who sign separate $500,000 contracts with one buyer are treated as a single $1 million conveyance.
  • Contract assignments are tested separately. A $900,000 contract assigned for $200,000 is treated as two conveyances, each below the line, when the parties are unrelated and the deal was not built to avoid the tax.
  • Mixed use. If a $1.5 million two-family house holds a $500,000 residential unit and a $1 million retail unit, the whole $1.5 million meets the threshold, but tax applies only to the $500,000 residential portion.

What extra transfer taxes apply in New York City?

New York City sales carry two more state taxes, both added from July 1, 2019. They are explained in the state's technical memorandum TSB-M-19(1)R.

The additional base tax is $1.25 per $500, paid by the seller. It applies to residential property at $3 million or more, and to other property at $2 million or more. The supplemental tax is paid by the buyer and applies to residential sales of $2 million or more, at tiered rates on the entire conveyance:

  • $2 million up to $3 million: 0.25%
  • $3 million up to $5 million: 0.5%
  • $5 million up to $10 million: 1.25%
  • $10 million up to $15 million: 2.25%
  • $15 million up to $20 million: 2.5%
  • $20 million up to $25 million: 2.75%
  • $25 million or more: 2.9%

The memorandum works one example through. On a $7 million New York City residence, the seller owes $28,000 of base tax plus $17,500 of additional base tax, $45,500 in all. The buyer owes $70,000 of mansion tax plus $87,500 of supplemental tax, $157,500 in all. The city also levies its own Real Property Transfer Tax, which the Department of Finance says is usually paid as part of closing costs. Ask the title closer for the current city rate on your sale.

When and where is the mansion tax paid?

The tax is due no later than the 15th day after the deed is delivered. Tax Law section 1410 sets that deadline, and it also bars a recording officer from recording the deed until the return is filed and the tax is paid.

For property outside New York City, the parties file Form TP-584 with the county clerk where the property sits. In the city they file Form TP-584-NYC, and the city's own transfer tax return is built online through ACRIS, the Automated City Register Information System. If a deed is not going to be recorded, the return and payment go straight to the Tax Department by the same 15-day deadline.

Three filing details can slow a closing. When a limited liability company is the seller or buyer of a building with up to four dwelling units, the filing must come with documents naming its members, managers and authorized persons, down to the individuals who own it. Nonresident sellers must compute their gain and pay any estimated income tax due, unless an exemption on the form applies. And the city's transfer tax return must be signed by both seller and buyer, or the one who did not sign may face non-filer penalties.

Which transfers avoid the mansion tax?

Governmental buyers are exempt, and so are transfers made without consideration. The Tax Department lists the nontaxable conveyances on its transfer tax page, and several matter to families selling a house:

  • A transfer by devise, bequest or inheritance is not a conveyance at all, so a house passing under a will or by intestacy does not trigger the tax at that step.
  • A bona fide gift made without consideration and unconnected to a sale is nontaxable.
  • A transfer given in connection with a tax sale is nontaxable.
  • Conveyances to a nonprofit that holds the land for conservation, parks or historic preservation are exempt from the mansion tax in particular.

A foreclosure or a deed in lieu of foreclosure, by contrast, falls inside the definition of a conveyance. An heir who later sells the inherited house at $1 million or more faces the tax on that sale like any other owner.

What should a New York seller check before a contract near $1 million?

Start with the contract language on who pays which tax, since the statute sets a default and the contract can shift the base tax. If the buyer agrees to pay the seller's transfer tax, the consideration grows by that amount, and both the base tax and the mansion tax rise with it.

Then ask the closing attorney or title company three things: whether the property fits the residential definition, whether any seller concession counts as added price, and who will file Form TP-584 and collect the buyer's payment at the table. Because the seller becomes jointly liable if the buyer does not pay, the filing should be confirmed before the deed is delivered.

More questions about New York Mansion Tax

Does the New York mansion tax apply to a $999,999 sale?

No, the tax applies only when the consideration for the entire conveyance is $1 million or more. Consideration includes assumed mortgages and obligations the buyer takes over for the seller, so a price just under the line can still cross it once those items are added. Related contracts for the same property are also combined.

Can the seller be forced to pay the mansion tax?

Yes, if the buyer does not pay or is exempt. Section 1402-a(b) then puts the duty on the seller, and the liability is joint and several, so the state may collect the full amount from either side. Confirm with the closing attorney that the buyer's payment is made with the return.

Is there a mansion tax on an inherited house?

Not on the transfer to the heir. The Tax Department says a conveyance by devise, bequest or inheritance is outside the definition of a conveyance. The tax can arise when the heir or estate later sells the house for $1 million or more.

How much is the mansion tax on a $1,500,000 house?

It is $15,000, which is 1 percent of the consideration. The state's FAQ publication applies the same 1 percent arithmetic to its examples, including a $1.2 million three-family house. The seller's separate base transfer tax is $2 per $500, and New York City sales add the city and state taxes described above.

Where do I file for the mansion tax?

Outside New York City, file Form TP-584 with the county clerk where the property is located, within 15 days after the deed is delivered. Inside the city, file Form TP-584-NYC, and prepare the city transfer tax packet online in ACRIS. Unrecorded deeds are filed directly with the Tax Department.

Enhanced STAR is for primary residences of seniors age 65+ with qualifying income of $110,750 or less for the 2026-27 school year and $113,550 or less for 2027-28; based on first $91,700 of full value for 2027-28. STAR applies only to school district taxes (except partly to city taxes in NYC, Buffalo, Rochester, Yonkers, Syracuse). (NYS DTF 'Types of STAR' (updated Oct 27, 2026); source)
  • STAR registration: register once via the Homeowner Benefit Portal in Individual Online Services; DTF issues the STAR credit payment each year if eligible. New homeowners should register as soon as the home becomes their primary residence. Update registration after ownership change (marriage, divorce, survivorship, trust, etc.); close registration if you sell the property. (NYS DTF 'Register for STAR' (updated July 14, 2026); source)
  • If BAR relief is denied: Small Claims Assessment Review (SCAR) for owner-occupied 1-3 family homes (or small vacant land), $30 fee; or tax certiorari in State Supreme Court under Article 7 of the Real Property Tax Law. Both must start within 30 days of filing of the final assessment roll or notice of filing, whichever is later. (NYS DTF 'Grievance procedures'; RPTL Art. 7; source)

What we could not confirm

  • What happens to your STAR benefit when you sell. Ask the Department of Taxation and Finance or the assessor.

New York STAR exemption FAQ

Do I need to register for STAR?

Yes. The state tells homeowners to register once through the Homeowner Benefit Portal, and new homeowners should register as soon as the home becomes their primary residence.

What is the Basic STAR income limit?

The Department of Taxation and Finance lists $500,000 for the Basic STAR credit and $250,000 for the exemption.

What is the STAR program in New York?

STAR is the School Tax Relief program, and it cuts the school tax on a house that the owner lives in as a primary residence. It comes in two levels: Basic STAR for any age, and Enhanced STAR for owners 65 and older with lower incomes.

The benefit reaches you in one of two forms. The STAR credit is a check or direct deposit from the state that you use to pay the school bill. The STAR exemption is a cut taken off the school bill itself. According to the Tax Department's eligibility page, the exemption is closed to new homeowners, while people who have received it since 2015 can keep it on the same primary residence.

For a seller, that split matters. If your house carries the exemption, your buyer will not inherit it, and a buyer who needs the benefit has to register for the credit.

Which taxes does STAR reduce?

STAR reduces school district taxes only. The Tax Department says it does not touch county, town or village bills, with one exception: in New York City, Buffalo, Rochester, Yonkers and Syracuse the benefit is split between city taxes and school taxes.

Many owners expect a larger drop than they get for this reason. A homeowner outside those five cities will see the savings only on the school portion of the combined tax statement. Senior citizens who receive STAR may also qualify for a separate senior citizens exemption, which is a separate program. Ask your local assessor how to apply for it.

What are the Basic and Enhanced STAR income limits?

Basic STAR has an income limit of $500,000 for the credit and $250,000 for the exemption, and it applies to the first $30,000 of a home's full value. Enhanced STAR is open to owners 65 and older with income of $110,750 or less for the 2026-27 school year and $113,550 or less for 2027-28.

STAR benefit levels listed by the NYS Department of Taxation and Finance (page updated October 27, 2026)
ItemBasic STAREnhanced STAR
Who qualifiesOwner-occupants of any ageResident owner age 65 or older
Income limit$500,000 (credit); $250,000 (exemption)$110,750 for 2026-27; $113,550 for 2027-28
Value coveredFirst $30,000 of full valueFirst $91,700 of full value for 2027-28

Income means federal adjusted gross income minus the taxable part of IRA distributions. The 2026 benefit is judged on the 2024 tax year, and the income counted belongs to resident owners and their resident spouses. Income of owners who do not live in the home is left out.

Who is eligible to receive STAR?

You must own the property, live in it as your primary residence, and meet the age and income test for the level you want. For a credit in any given year, you need to own the home and live in it as of July 1 of that year.

  • Houses, condominiums, cooperative apartments, manufactured homes and farm houses can qualify.
  • A married couple gets only one STAR benefit, however many properties they own, unless they are legally separated.
  • Someone buying under a land contract (an executory contract of sale) counts as an owner.
  • Corporations, partnerships and LLCs are not eligible unless the property is a farm dwelling.
  • A nursing home resident who owns the home can still qualify if no one besides a co-owner or spouse lives there.

The state looks at how long you spend at the property each year, where you are registered to vote, and the address on your vehicle registrations and government IDs. The Tax Department can ask for proof of residency.

How do trusts, life estates and surviving spouses fit in?

A person who put the home in a trust but still lives there as the trust beneficiary is treated as the owner and gets the STAR benefit. Under a life estate, the life tenant is deemed the owner for STAR purposes, so eligibility turns on the life tenant's own age and income.

A surviving spouse can keep an Enhanced STAR benefit earned by the late spouse if the survivor reaches 62 by December 31 of the year of death. A younger survivor receives Basic STAR until turning 65 and then moves to Enhanced STAR if otherwise eligible.

These cases come up after a death in the family. If you are handling an inherited house, check how title is held before you list it, because a change of ownership means the STAR registration should be updated or closed.

How do you register for the STAR credit?

You register once through the Homeowner Benefit Portal inside your Individual Online Services account with the Tax Department. After logging in, open the Services menu, choose Real property tax, then Homeowner Benefit Portal, and select Register.

Have these items ready before you begin:

  • names and Social Security numbers for all owners and their spouses
  • the name of your school district and the approximate purchase date
  • the most recent school tax bill, if the current owners received one
  • 2024 federal or state income tax returns for all owners
  • the legal name of the trust, if one holds title

Sellers' names are optional but can help you receive the credit before school taxes come due. Write down the confirmation number, because the Tax Department will ask for it if you call. If you pay school tax through a mortgage escrow account, tell the lender or its agent when you switch from the exemption to the credit.

What should you do with your STAR registration when you sell?

Close it. The Tax Department says that if you sell the property or no longer want the benefit, you should close the registration from the Homeowner Benefit Portal. You do not register again each year, and the state reviews your information annually and issues the credit automatically when you remain eligible.

Update the registration instead of closing it if ownership changes through marriage, divorce, a co-owner giving up an interest, survivorship, a trust, a life estate or a name change.

Buyers have their own task. A new owner who is not yet receiving STAR should register as soon as the house becomes the primary residence, and the Tax Department publishes a one-page handout for realtors and attorneys to give to purchasers. Ask the assessor in your county whether any local exemption on the house is removed at sale, since local exemptions are handled separately from STAR.

What happens to STAR and other exemptions at a closing?

STAR stays with the owner who registered, so it does not pass to the buyer through the deed. The state-level step is simple: the seller closes the registration and the buyer registers for the credit.

Local exemptions work through the county. Take Nassau County's North Hempstead as an example: the town's closing guide says exemptions are generally not transferable at closing and that buyers should apply with the county Department of Assessment. It also warns that when an exemption is removed after a sale, the county may add prorated restored taxes to a later bill, up to one year's worth, and that this can take up to two years to appear.

The practical lesson holds across the state. Before you sign, ask your closing attorney or the county assessor which exemptions are on the house, and ask whether a restored-tax charge could follow the sale. A buyer who is counting on the exemption in the price should hear the answer before the contract is final.

More questions about New York STAR Exemption

Can a new buyer get the STAR exemption on a house in New York?

No. The exemption is closed to new homeowners, and the Tax Department says people who have received it since 2015 can continue only for the same primary residence. A buyer registers for the STAR credit once the house is their primary residence.

Do I need to register for STAR every year?

No. You register once, and the Tax Department issues the credit each year as long as you stay eligible. You only update the registration when ownership changes, and you close it if you sell.

What is the Enhanced STAR income limit for 2027-28?

It is $113,550 or less. For the 2026-27 school year the limit is $110,750, and at least one resident owner must be 65 or older by December 31 of the benefit year.

Does STAR lower my county or town tax?

No. It applies only to school district taxes, except in New York City, Buffalo, Rochester, Yonkers and Syracuse, where the benefit is applied partly to city taxes and partly to school taxes.

Can an LLC or a corporation receive STAR?

No, unless the property is a farm dwelling. The state limits the benefit to eligible individual owners who live in the home, and a trust beneficiary who lives there is treated as the owner.

New York property tax is set and collected locally, so due dates and assessors differ by town, city and county. This guide covers the statewide rules we confirmed and points to local guides.

STAR

  • STAR: Basic STAR is for owner-occupied primary residences; income limit $500,000 for the Basic STAR credit ($250,000 for the Basic STAR exemption); based on the first $30,000 of full value. Enhanced STAR is for primary residences of seniors age 65+ with qualifying income of $110,750 or less for the 2026-27 school year and $113,550 or less for 2027-28; based on first $91,700 of full value for 2027-28. STAR applies only to school district taxes (except partly to city taxes in NYC, Buffalo, Rochester, Yonkers, Syracuse). (NYS DTF 'Types of STAR' (updated Oct 27, 2026); source)
  • STAR registration: register once via the Homeowner Benefit Portal in Individual Online Services; DTF issues the STAR credit payment each year if eligible. New homeowners should register as soon as the home becomes their primary residence. Update registration after ownership change (marriage, divorce, survivorship, trust, etc.); close registration if you sell the property. (NYS DTF 'Register for STAR' (updated July 14, 2026); source)

Tax liens and unpaid tax

  • RPTL 1110: real property subject to a delinquent tax lien may be redeemed by paying the enforcing officer the lien amount plus lawful charges on or before the end of the redemption period; the redemption period expires two years after lien date, though tax districts may lengthen it for residential/farm property (RPTL 1111) or shorten it to one year for vacant and abandoned residential property (1111-a), and a published notice (1124) may specify a later date. (NY RPTL §1110(1)-(2) (rev. 2019-12-27); source)
  • NYC tax lien sale: City sells unpaid property tax/water-sewer/other charge liens to a single authorized buyer (not the public); it is not a sale of the property but can lead to foreclosure. Lienholder may charge a 5% surcharge plus interest compounded daily at 6% (assessed value <= $250,000), 9% ($250,000-$450,000) or 16% (> $450,000), plus ~$300 admin costs. Foreclosure may begin within one year after the sale if unpaid. Eligibility e.g. 1-family owner-occupied: $5,000 property tax debt (3 years). 2025 sale held June 3, 2025. 5% surcharge waiver for primary-residence owners with combined income no greater than $110,750. (NYC Dept of Finance, Lien sales page; source)
  • Transfers given in connection with a tax sale are nontaxable conveyances for state transfer tax purposes. (NYS DTF real estate transfer tax page; source)

New York property tax FAQ

When is Grievance Day in New York?

In most communities it is the fourth Tuesday in May. Suffolk and Westchester use different days, and NYC uses its own Tax Commission dates.

What is the redemption period on a New York tax lien?

RPTL 1110 sets a two-year redemption period for a delinquent tax lien, starting from the lien date.

Who sets and collects property tax across New York?

Bills in this state come from local governments, so the office you pay and the dates you follow turn on the county, city, town, village and school district around the house. State law sets the common rules for challenging an assessment, claiming relief and handling delinquent taxes. The local assessor and the local collecting office supply the numbers.

Who enforces unpaid tax also varies. Under Real Property Tax Law section 1102, the enforcing officer is the county treasurer or commissioner of finance where the county is the tax district, the official named in the charter in a city, the village treasurer in a village, and the town supervisor in a town, unless another law says otherwise.

A homeowner preparing to sell should learn early which office holds the current bill and any back balance. The closing agent will go to that same office for the figures.

How can an owner contest an assessment here?

Hand the complaint to the assessor ahead of the review board's hearing, or to the board in person on hearing day. Under section 524, nothing can be filed at a continued hearing, while anything in by the original hearing date counts as timely.

Hearings open on the fourth Tuesday of May, except where a charter, county tax act or special law picks another date. Section 512 also lets an assessing unit that shares an assessor with another unit adopt a local law moving the first hearing date between the fourth Tuesday of May and the second Tuesday of June.

Three points shape a strong complaint:

  • The grounds are limited to an assessment that is excessive, unequal or unlawful, or a property placed in the wrong class.
  • Outside cities of five million or more, the complaint goes on the commissioner's prescribed form, with a statement of the reduction sought and an estimate of the property's value.
  • If the assessor and the owner both sign the statement on the form, it becomes a stipulation to the assessed value. When that figure is entered on the final roll, the owner gives up court review under Article 7.

Where a town or city raises an assessment, section 510 requires a mailed notice, sent within the window that starts 120 days before the tentative roll is due and ends ten days before the hearing, and it has to list when the board meets. A missed mailing does not stop the tax from being levied. New York City follows its own charter on notices.

What can an owner do after a denied complaint?

The owner can petition the Supreme Court, though the window is brief. Section 702 says the case must begin inside thirty days of the final roll being completed and filed, and a late petition gets dismissed.

The roll is not considered finally completed until the last day the law sets for filing it or until notice has been given as required, whichever comes later. Since the thirty days run from that date, get the filing date from the assessor instead of guessing.

A seller who is mid-contract should tell the closing attorney about any pending complaint or court filing.

What does STAR cover, and who gets it?

STAR is the state's school tax relief program. The tax department lays out two versions on its Types of STAR page, updated October 27, 2026.

New York STAR benefit types (source: NYS Department of Taxation and Finance, Types of STAR)
BenefitWho it servesIncome limitValue basis
Basic STARHomes the owner lives in as a primary residence$500,000 (credit) or $250,000 (exemption)First $30,000 of full value
Enhanced STARPrimary residences of owners age 65 and older$110,750 for 2026-2027 and $113,550 for 2027-2028First $91,700 of full value for 2027-2028

The savings come off school levies. County, town and city bills stay as they are, with five exceptions: New York City, Buffalo, Rochester, Yonkers and Syracuse split the exemption between city and school bills. Seniors who receive STAR may also qualify for the senior citizens exemption.

What should buyers and sellers do about STAR?

Register once through the Homeowner Benefit Portal in your Individual Online Services account. The Tax Department then issues the STAR credit each year for as long as you remain eligible, according to its STAR registration page.

A new owner registers once the house becomes the primary home. The registration form asks for these items:

  • names and Social Security numbers for all owners and their spouses;
  • the school district and a rough purchase date;
  • the sellers' names, which are optional but may help the credit arrive before school taxes are due;
  • the most recent school tax bill, if the current owners received one;
  • the legal name of any trust that holds title;
  • federal or state income tax returns for all owners.

The same portal lets an owner edit or close a registration, which is the step a seller takes after the house is gone. Enrolling in direct deposit and switching from the exemption to the credit are also handled there.

Is there a senior citizen exemption in New York?

Yes, but a municipality has to choose to offer it. Real Property Tax Law section 467 lets a local governing board, after a public hearing, adopt a law exempting up to 50 percent of assessed value of property owned by people 65 and older. The statute also covers a married couple or siblings when one of them is 65 or older.

The exemption scales down as income rises, and municipalities can raise the income ceiling by local law. Because each county, city, town and school district decides separately, ask the local assessor whether the exemption is offered, what the income cap is, and when the application is due. Do not assume the neighboring town follows the same rules.

What follows when a tax bill goes unpaid?

Unpaid tax turns into a delinquent lien. Owners get the property back by paying the enforcing officer the lien amount and lawful charges, and section 1110 sets the cutoff at two years from the lien date.

Three things can move that cutoff:

  • A tax district may lengthen it for residential or farm property.
  • A district may shorten it to one year for residential property placed on a vacant and abandoned list before the taxes went delinquent.
  • A published foreclosure notice may name a later expiration date, and then that date controls.

Charges are part of the delinquent tax. Section 1102 counts interest, penalties, notice and publication costs, and recording costs among them. It treats up to $250 per parcel, or 2 percent of the taxes, interest and penalties due, whichever is greater, as a reasonable foreclosure-related charge without further proof. After redemption, the enforcing officer will issue a certificate of redemption on request, and filing it with the county clerk cancels the notice of pendency for that parcel.

Can a house be sold while tax is owed?

Redemption means paying the enforcing officer the lien amount plus charges, so the money has to arrive before the redemption window closes. A sale gives the owner a way to do that, with the title company sending the payoff from the proceeds.

Request the figure early, in writing. Deeds given in a tax sale are listed as nontaxable conveyances on the state's real estate transfer tax page.

Contact the county treasurer, city finance office, or town or village tax office for the amount and the deadline. A close deadline belongs in the first conversation with any buyer.

More questions about New York Property Tax Guide

When do assessment hearings begin?

Usually the fourth Tuesday of May, which many people call Grievance Day. A charter, county tax act or special law can pick another date, and a unit that shares its assessor may start as late as the second Tuesday of June. Your assessor can give the exact date.

Will STAR reduce my county or town bill?

No. It lowers school levies. Only New York City, Buffalo, Rochester, Yonkers and Syracuse apply part of the exemption to city taxes. County and town bills elsewhere stay the same.

How long after a lien is the redemption deadline?

Two years from the lien date in the standard case. A district may lengthen the period for residential property, cut it to one year for vacant and abandoned residential property, or publish a later date in its foreclosure notice. The enforcing officer can confirm which applies.

What is the deadline to sue over an assessment in New York?

A court proceeding to review an assessment must start within thirty days after the final assessment roll is completed and filed. Signing a stipulation with the assessor on the complaint form ends court review for that year. Talk to a New York attorney about the exact date before it passes.

Should a seller close the STAR registration?

Yes, update or close it in the Homeowner Benefit Portal once the house is sold. The buyer registers separately when the house becomes a primary home. Giving the buyer the sellers' names on that form can help the credit arrive before school taxes are due.
